fixes.explanation: God says, "So I will make them jealous by those who are not a people; I will make them angry by a nation without understanding." (Deuteronomy 32:21). Look at how the verse is built. They provoked Him with "that which is not God," and the reply comes through "those who are not a people." The two halves match.

Nobody at the altar is named here, friend. God says, "…I will make them jealous by those who are not a people; I will make them angry by a nation without understanding." (Deuteronomy 32:21). The verse points to a people who are not a people, and to a nation without understanding. Priests and altars don't come up in these lines.

God says, "I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal, and there is no one who can deliver from My hand." (Deuteronomy 32:39). No one at all. Death and life, wounding and healing, and nobody who can pull anyone out of His hand.

This one is true, friend. The song says, "But the LORD’s portion is His people, Jacob His allotted inheritance." (Deuteronomy 32:9). The portion is His people, and the song names Jacob. Out of everything there is, that's what the LORD calls His own.

Hebron isn't in this song, friend. Moses sings, "He found him in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness…" (Deuteronomy 32:10). No valley here. I've lived in a junk drawer, and a howling wilderness still sounds rougher. And right there in it, the song says, "He guarded him as the apple of His eye."

The song says, "He abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation." (Deuteronomy 32:15). Jeshurun is described as fat, bloated and gorged, and then he walks away from the One who made him. I think being stuffed can give a person a very short memory.

Moses sings, "They sacrificed to demons, not to God, to gods they had not known…" (Deuteronomy 32:17). Gods they had not known. They gave their offerings to those instead of to God. That's a heavy part of the song.

The song doesn't say stars, friend. It says, "They sacrificed to demons, not to God…" (Deuteronomy 32:17). The verse goes on to call them gods they had not known. That's a heavy line, and the song says it plainly.

Not old, friend. The song calls them "…newly arrived gods, which your fathers did not fear." (Deuteronomy 32:17). They were newly arrived, and even the fathers hadn't feared them. So old gods isn't what the song says.

God says, "I will hide My face from them; I will see what will be their end." (Deuteronomy 32:20). He goes on, "For they are a perverse generation—children of unfaithfulness." I think this one hurts to hear. It's a heavy line.

A small army is a fair guess, friend. But look at how Moses asks it: "How could one man pursue a thousand, or two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up?" (Deuteronomy 32:30). The song's answer is that it takes the LORD giving them up. The size of the army isn't what the song points to.

Old weapons would be a fair guess. But the song never brings up weapons. It asks how one could chase a thousand "…unless the LORD had given them up?" (Deuteronomy 32:30). The way the question is built, it happens only if the LORD had given them up.

Mountains feel like the sturdiest thing around, friend, but God doesn't point to them here. He declares, "As surely as I live forever…" (Deuteronomy 32:40). All the weight of the words sits on Him living forever.
